strengths: The problem addressed—fixed-viewpoint occlusion and task interference in multi-task manipulation—is real and well-motivated, and the motivation is clearly illustrated (Fig. 1).

The proposed framework combines two orthogonal ideas: RL-based active viewpoint selection (MVEP) and a task-aware MoE encoder (TaskMoE), and the pseudo-environment interaction mechanism that avoids expensive simulator rollouts during PPO training is a clever and practical engineering contribution.

Evaluation breadth is reasonably good: 18 RLBench tasks with comparisons against RVT2, ARP, and ARP+, plus ablations, sensitivity analysis over view count and radial constraints, an efficiency/latency analysis, zero-shot generalization on an unseen task, and qualitative real-robot results on a Dobot Xtrainer platform.

Per-task analysis supports the central claim: the largest gains occur on occlusion-prone tasks (e.g., insert peg 96.0 vs. 78.4; put in cupboard 76.0 vs. 69.6; put in safe 92.0 vs. 86.4), which is consistent with the mechanism the authors propose.

The methodology is mostly described at sufficient detail for a follow-up (camera pose parameterization, reward terms, three-stage training), and a hyperparameter table and algorithm are included in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline average improvement is modest: 86.7% vs. 84.9% for ARP+ (+1.8 points) over only 25 evaluation episodes per task, with no confidence intervals, variance over seeds, or statistical significance testing. Given this margin, claims of 'significantly outperforms' are not well supported.

Evaluation protocols are inconsistent across experiments. The main results (Appendix C) use 100 demonstrations per task, while the quantitative analysis section states 20 demonstration episodes per task; consequently Table 3 averages (~49.6%) are not comparable to Table 1 (~86.7%). This fragmentation weakens the evidential chain and suggests cherry-pickable setups.

The 'w/o Active Exploration (Random Viewpoints)' ablation reporting 8.89% success is suspicious and not properly explained. Random viewpoints yielding near-total failure while task performance under the reduced validation setup reaches ~50% suggests a train/test mismatch confound (e.g., the model fine-tuned only with dynamic views degenerates without them) rather than a clean measure of view-planning value.
The claimed 'up to +56% improvement' is unclear and appears inflated—comparing per-task numbers, the largest delta is insert peg (+17.6 points, ~22% relative); no task shows a 56-point gap over ARP+.

TaskMoE's contribution is small (86.67% vs. 85.56% without it, ~1.1 points) and its novelty is limited: it combines standard MoE with cross-attention routing and FiLM conditioning, and the gate-count decoupling (NG < NJ) is a heuristic without analysis of learned task clusters or routing behavior.

The RL reward design raises technical questions that are not resolved: the primary reward r0 = Lref − LTAVP compares losses against a frozen reference model, which could be gamed or degenerate; how the 'learnable component weights' wi in Eq. (9) are optimized is never specified; and the pseudo-environment mechanism (deferred to a short appendix algorithm) lacks detail on how rendered views from novel poses are supervised without environment interaction.

Average success is not uniformly improved: TAVP regresses on several tasks vs. ARP+ (e.g., stack cups 60.0 vs. 80.0, open drawer 88.0 vs. 92.8, push buttons/sweep ties or drops), and this regression is not analyzed.
Real-world evaluation is purely qualitative (Fig. 7 shows only rollouts with no success rates, episode counts, or baselines), so the real-robot claims are anecdotal.

Presentation quality issues: a duplicated paragraph on Gaussian viewpoint modeling in the MVEP section, inconsistent terminology (MVEP vs. MVEPN, ARP vs. 'APR'), a stray watermark text in Fig. 1, and general polish problems that suggest a rushed submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: fixed viewpoints cause occlusion in manipulation, and multi-task policies suffer from feature interference. The proposed combination of active viewpoint selection (MVEP) with a task-aware Mixture-of-Experts (TaskMoE) is a coherent system design.

The pseudo-environment interaction mechanism, which derives RL rewards from reference-vs-policy loss differences on offline demonstration data instead of costly simulator rollouts, is an interesting engineering contribution for making viewpoint-policy training tractable.

The evaluation is comparatively broad for this area: 18 RLBench tasks, ablations of both main components, sensitivity analysis over the number of views and radial constraints, an inference-time comparison (10.7% latency overhead, Table 4), and a supplementary real-robot study on a two-arm platform.

The writing and figures are generally clear; the three-stage training pipeline and camera pose parameterization are described in enough detail to be reproducible in principle, and code is stated to be released.
weaknesses: The headline empirical gains are marginal and partially contradicted by the paper's own claims. The average improvement over the strongest baseline ARP+ is only +1.8% (86.7 vs 84.9, Table 1), yet the text states TAVP 'achieves substantially higher success rates across all tasks.' In fact TAVP underperforms ARP+ on several tasks (Place Cups 44.0 vs 48.8, Stack Cups 60.0 vs 80.0, Open Drawer 88.0 vs 92.8, Sweep to Dustpan 92.0 vs 97.6, Screw Bulb 88.0 vs 89.6). This overclaiming undermines confidence in the results.

Statistical support is weak. Each task is evaluated over only 25 episodes with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Given per-task differences of a few percentage points and 25 trials, most of the reported per-task comparisons (including the claimed +56% on specific tasks) cannot be judged reliable.

The ablation in Table 2 is not a clean comparison. Removing active exploration drops success from 86.67% to 8.89%, but it is unclear whether the random-viewpoint model is trained with the same Stage 2/3 procedure or is a differently constructed baseline; a collapse of this magnitude suggests a confound (e.g., train/test viewpoint distribution mismatch) rather than evidence that exploration is 'dominant.' Moreover, the ablation text reports 86.44% for full TAVP while Table 2 reports 86.67%, an unexplained numerical inconsistency.

The TaskMoE contribution is weakly supported. Removing it costs only ~1.1% (85.56 vs 86.67), and the zero-shot 'generalization' claim rests on a single unseen task (Open drawer) at 12% success vs 0% without TaskMoE, with 25 episodes. One task at 12% success is far from demonstrating the claimed generalization capability, and Open drawer is among the training tasks in the main 18-task benchmark, which makes the experimental setup confusing.

Novelty is limited and the delta over prior work is unclear. MoE routing conditioned on instructions/scenes exists (e.g., language-guided sparse MoE [10], SDP [14]), and active viewpoint selection for manipulation is a well-studied idea. The paper does not empirically compare against any active-perception or alternative MoE routing baseline; all comparisons are against dense fixed-view models (RVT2/ARP/ARP+).

Key methodological details are deferred or under-specified. The pseudo-environment mechanism (the core of Stage 2) is only sketched in an appendix algorithm; the reward r0 = Lref - L_TAVP is computed by the same network being trained, raising unaddressed concerns about reward hacking (e.g., inflating reference loss or degrading the frozen reference's predictions is impossible, but exploiting loss-reducing yet uninformative viewpoints is). How re-rendered novel views obtained from a reconstructed point cloud are realized on the physical robot is not explained; the real-world section only shows executions from fixed cameras, leaving a gap between the simulation method and the real-world evidence.

Presentation lapses suggest insufficient polish: references [1]-[6] are placeholder/template entries ('frobnicatable foo filter') left in the bibliography, and the name 'Zhouxia' appears as a watermark inside Figures 1 and 3, which is both sloppy and an anonymity concern for a double-blind submission.

The evaluation protocol itself differs between the main results (100 demos/task training, full 18-task setting) and the quantitative analysis (20 demos/task on a 5-task subset), making Tables 3 and 5 hard to reconcile with Table 1 and limiting the sensitivity analysis's relevance to the headline results.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: fixed camera viewpoints cause occlusion and incomplete observations in multi-task manipulation, and the qualitative examples (Fig. 1, Fig. 4) illustrate this clearly.

The framework is reasonably complete, combining active viewpoint exploration (MVEP trained with PPO and a pseudo-environment to avoid costly simulator rollouts) with a task-aware MoE encoder (TaskMoE) featuring cross-modal routing and a decoupled gate design (NG < NJ), which is a sensible scalability idea.

Evaluation breadth is good: 18 RLBench tasks with fixed-view dense baselines (RVT2, ARP, ARP+), ablations (Table 2), sensitivity analyses on view count K and radial constraints (Table 3), an inference-time comparison (Table 4, only ~10.7% latency overhead), a zero-shot test on one unseen task (Table 5), and a real-world demonstration on a dual-arm platform across 5 tasks.
The pseudo-environment interaction mechanism (Algorithm 1) that reuses demonstration data for offline policy optimization of viewpoint selection is a practical contribution to training efficiency.
The paper is generally readable, with a clear three-stage training pipeline and reasonable implementation details (hyperparameters in Table 6).
weaknesses: The headline improvement is modest and mixed: average success rises only from 84.9% (ARP+) to 86.7%, and TAVP actually underperforms the strongest baseline on several tasks (Place Cups 48.8 vs 48.8/44.0, Screw Bulb 89.6 vs 88.0, Stack Cups 80.0 vs 60.0, Sweep to Dustpan 97.6 vs 92.0, Turn Tap 100.0 vs 96.0, Open Drawer 92.8 vs 88.0). The claim that TAVP 'achieves substantially higher success rates across all tasks' is factually inaccurate, and no statistical significance testing, error bars, or multi-seed results are reported despite only 25 evaluation episodes per task.

The claimed contribution of TaskMoE is internally inconsistent: Table 2 reports that removing TaskMoE costs only 1.1 points (86.67 -> 85.56), while Table 5 reports more than a doubling of success (49.6 vs 24.0) on the 5-task validation setup. Although the setups differ (100 vs 20 demos/task), this discrepancy is not explained, and it materially weakens the evidence that task-aware routing is a key driver of performance.

The 'w/o Active Exploration (Random Viewpoints)' ablation collapsing to 8.89% does not cleanly isolate the value of learned view planning: random views are out-of-distribution for a downstream model trained on explored views, so this number likely conflates distribution shift with the benefit of task-aware viewpoint selection. A stronger control (e.g., a fixed set of 'good' hand-designed or oracle viewpoints, or fixed-view training with the same re-rendered-view architecture) is missing.

Quantitative claims in the text do not match the tables: the claimed 'up to +56% improvement' for put-in-cupboard/insert-peg is not derivable from Table 1 (69.6->76.0 and 78.4->96.0), and the stated '4%' increments for close jar / meat off grill / slide block are also inconsistent (these are 4.8-7.2 points). The abstract/tables also report 86.7% while Table 2 reports 86.44% for the full model.

Real-world experiments are qualitative only: no success rates, episode counts, or baseline comparison numbers are provided for the 5 real tasks, so the real-robot claims of superiority over ARP+ are anecdotal (Fig. 4/7).

Novelty is moderate: the pipeline is largely assembled from existing components (RVT-2 coarse grounding, ARP autoregressive action head, standard MoE, FiLM, look-at parameterization, PPO), and the incremental designs (cross-attention routing, decoupled gates) are not deeply analyzed (e.g., no visualization of learned gate/expert assignments to support the claimed 'latent task clusters').

Technical presentation has issues: page 4 contains duplicated paragraphs describing the Gaussian pose parameterization; PPO is described alongside a reparameterization trick in a way that conflates on-policy likelihood-ratio updates with differentiable sampling; 'MVEP' vs 'MVEPN' naming is inconsistent; key details of the pseudo-environment and learnable reward weights (which could destabilize PPO) are deferred to supplementary material.

The reference list contains leftover CVPR template placeholder entries ([1]-[6], 'F. LastName, frobnicatable foo filter'), and there are typos ('APR[79]' for ARP, 'Resutls'), which signal insufficient care in preparing the final manuscript.
Zero-shot generalization evidence is thin: a single unseen task at 12% success is far from demonstrating the claimed generalization capability of TaskMoE.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important problem: fixed camera viewpoints in VLA/multi-task manipulation cause occlusion and incomplete observations. The motivation (Fig. 1) is clear and the idea of combining active view planning with task-aware routing is coherent.

The Multi-Viewpoint Exploration Policy is trained via a 'pseudo-environment' interaction mechanism (Algorithm 1) that derives RL rewards from reference-model losses on offline demonstrations, avoiding costly physical simulation rollouts — a practical engineering contribution.

The evaluation is broad in scope: 18 RLBench tasks, real-world experiments on 5 tasks with a physical robot, ablations (Table 2), sensitivity to view count and radial bounds (Table 3), inference latency (Table 5), zero-shot transfer (Table 6), robustness testing under occlusion/illumination (Table 7), and data efficiency (Table 8).

The TaskMoE design (decoupled number of gates from number of tasks, NG < NJ, instruction/scene-conditioned routing via cross-attention + FiLM) is a sensible attempt to address task interference and generalization to unseen tasks.
The ablation showing that active view planning is the dominant factor (8.89% with random views, 83.33% with fixed views, 86.67% full) supports the central claim that viewpoint quality matters.
weaknesses: Marginal and inconsistent gains over the strongest baseline. The average improvement over ARP+ is only 1.7 points (84.9% -> 86.6%), and the text claims 'substantially higher success rates across all tasks,' which is contradicted by Table 1: TAVP is clearly worse on Put in Safe (78.0 vs 86.4), Stack Cups (64.0 vs 80.0), Place Wine (92.0 vs 96.0), and Close Jar gains are within noise (100 vs 100 for RVT2). Several TAVP results have large variance (e.g., 74.0±8.5 on Put in Cupboard), and no statistical significance analysis is provided.

Internal inconsistency in reported results undermines credibility. Table 3 reports an average success rate of 49.6% (K=3) on five tasks including Put item in drawer (32.0) and Turn tap (92.0), while Table 1 reports 100.0 and 100.0 respectively for the same tasks. The paper explains only that validation used 20 demonstrations, but this drastic discrepancy is not reconciled, and it is unclear which configuration the headline numbers use.

The headline ablation comparing against 'Random Viewpoints' (8.89%) is a strawman; the meaningful comparison is the fixed-viewpoint fine-tuned variant (83.33%), which shows the total benefit of active view planning is ~3.3 points. TaskMoE contributes only ~1.1 points (86.67 vs 85.56), which is weak support for the extensive claims made about it.

The zero-shot generalization claim (Table 6) is questionable: the 'unseen' task 'Open drawer' is semantically nearly identical to trained tasks ('open the top drawer', 'put the item in the top drawer' are among the 18 training tasks per Figure 8), so 12% success on this 'new task' hardly demonstrates OOD generalization; and it is evaluated on a single task with 25 episodes.

The real-world deployment of active view planning is under-specified. The method re-renders observations from predicted viewpoints of the point cloud, but on the real robot it is unclear how the physically mounted cameras realize the optimized poses (e.g., whether the wrist camera must physically move, and how this time/motion cost is handled). Inference latency (0.436s, +10.7% over ARP+) likely does not capture the cost of camera repositioning, and the real-world baseline is only Diffusion Policy, omitting stronger available baselines (RVT-2, ARP+) that the architecture is built upon.

The fairness of the comparison is a concern: TAVP incorporates RVT-2's coarse grounding, the ARP backbone, TaskMoE, and MVEP, so gains over ARP+ conflate the view-planning contribution with architectural additions; an ablation of TAVP evaluated at ARP+ capacity with fixed views is needed.

Carelessness in the manuscript: references [1]-[6] are template placeholder entries ('The frobnicatable foo filter', 'Frobnication'), the name 'Zhouxia' (an author name) is left embedded inside Figure 3, typos such as 'MVEPN', and the code link is a bare placeholder 'TAVP'. These indicate the submission was not carefully checked, which is a material professionalism issue at a top venue.

The 'novel pseudo-environment' is essentially computing a loss-difference reward (r0 = Lref − LTAVP) on offline data with PPO; since the action policy is frozen, there is a risk the view policy optimizes representations the frozen policy prefers rather than genuinely better viewpoints, and the theoretical justification for why this offline surrogate avoids distribution shift is not analyzed.

The sensitivity analysis in Table 3 is conducted on a different training regime (20 demos) than the main results, so its conclusions (e.g., tighter radial range improving 49.6% -> 56.0%) may not transfer to the main configuration, where the default range is retained despite the tighter range reportedly being better.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem: fixed viewpoints in multi-task VLA/imitation-learning pipelines cause occlusion and incomplete scene understanding, and active, task-aware view selection is a sensible remedy.

The evaluation is broad in scope: 18 RLBench tasks plus 5 real-robot tasks, with ablations (Table 2), parameter sensitivity (Table 3), inference-latency comparison (Table 5), a small zero-shot test (Table 6), robustness configurations (Table 7), and a data-efficiency study (Table 8). The 3-stage training recipe (supervised fixed-view training → PPO fine-tuning of MVEP with a pseudo-environment → final fine-tuning) is coherent and described end-to-end.

The pseudo-environment interaction (Algorithm 1), which computes rewards from loss differences against a frozen reference policy on offline demonstration data, is a practical way to avoid costly simulator interaction during view-policy optimization, and the paper reports a reasonable inference overhead (+~10.7% vs. ARP+).

Reporting is generally transparent on negative details, e.g., degraded performance on some tasks (Put in Safe 78.0, Stack Cups 64.0) and the small contribution of TaskMoE in the ablation (86.67 → 85.56 without it).
weaknesses: Claims are contradicted by the paper's own tables, which materially undermines trust. Section 4.2 states TAVP 'achieves substantially higher success rates across all tasks' compared to ARP+, yet TAVP is clearly worse on Put in Safe (78.0 vs. 96.0/97.6), Stack Cups (64.0 vs. 80.0), Sweep to Dustpan (92.0 vs. 100.0), and Close Jar is a tie. The claimed '+56% improvement' for put-in-cupboard-type tasks does not match the table (74.0 vs. ARP+ 69.6 is +4.4 points). These are not presentation nits; the headline narrative is overstated.

The overall gain over the strongest baseline is small: 86.6 vs. 84.9 for ARP+ (~1.7 points), and the ablation shows TaskMoE—presented as one of two core contributions—accounts for only ~1.1 points, with the rest attributable to view planning. Meanwhile the baseline comparison is arguably unfair: TAVP inherits RVT-2's coarse grounding and ARP's action policy and adds extra expert capacity (16 experts, 8 gates), while baselines are not given comparable capacity or additional components. There is no experiment isolating view planning at matched capacity against ARP+.

Evidence for the generalization claims is thin. The zero-shot analysis uses a single unseen task ('Open drawer'), 25 episodes, and a 12% success rate (vs. 0% without TaskMoE). This is far from sufficient support for statements that TaskMoE 'endows the model with the ability to generalize learned knowledge to new tasks.' The gates-vs-tasks decoupling (NG=8 < NJ=18) is a modest design change, and the semantics of the learned task clusters are never analyzed or visualized.

Evaluation protocols are inconsistent across experiments in ways that prevent cross-checking: the main benchmark uses 100 demonstrations/task while the quantitative analysis (Tables 3 and 6) uses 20/task, so results for the same tasks are wildly different (e.g., Put item in drawer is 100.0 in Table 1 but 32.0 in Table 3). The sensitivity analysis that 'selects' a tighter radial range as better (56.0 vs. 49.6) risks being tuned on the same five evaluation tasks with no held-out confirmation.

The ablation reporting is confusing and possibly erroneous: 'w/o Active Exploration Fine-tuning (Random Viewpoints)' collapses to 8.89%, but randomly chosen viewpoints within the valid spherical range should plausibly still outperform a poorly trained policy or at least behave sensibly relative to the fixed-view 83.33% setting; the relationship between these two rows and the training procedure is not explained. The reward design (r0 = Lref − LTAVP with learnable weights, online normalization, clipping to [−10,10]) is presented without any analysis of stability or learned weight values, and the pseudo-environment details are deferred to a brief appendix.

Reproducibility and polish fall short of the bar: the code link in the abstract is a placeholder ('TAVP'), and the bibliography contains unfilled template dummy entries ([1]–[6], 'The frobnicatable foo filter', 'Frobnication'), indicating a rushed submission. The real-world setup text says a 'single-arm (right arm) 6-DoF Dobot Nova 2' while Figure 4 depicts two arms and three RealSense cameras, and the setup section mentions five tasks whereas Figure 6 shows different task names.

The core mechanism has a structural caveat that is underexamined: TAVP does not move real cameras but re-renders views from an aggregated point cloud, so its 'dynamic views' are limited by depth-sensing quality—the paper itself concedes failure on reflective/transparent objects—yet the motivating figure presents re-rendering as if the robot physically acquires new viewpoints. Related work on active viewpoint selection for manipulation exists and the delta over it is not clearly delineated.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: fixed-viewpoint limitations in multi-task VLA models. The proposed TAVP framework combines active view planning (MVEP) with task-aware expert routing (TaskMoE), and the two components are reasonably motivated and complementary.

The pseudo-environment interaction mechanism (Algorithm 1) is a sensible practical contribution: it enables PPO-based viewpoint policy optimization using offline demonstrations rather than costly simulator rollouts, which is a useful engineering insight for the community.

Evaluation breadth is good: 18 RLBench tasks with comparisons against a broad set of baselines (PerAct, RVT, Act3D, 3D Diffuser Actor, RVT-2, ARP/ARP+), plus real-robot experiments on 5 tasks, robustness testing under occlusion/illumination variation, data-efficiency analysis, and inference-latency reporting.

Ablations cover the main components: removing TaskMoE and replacing active viewpoints with random viewpoints isolate the contribution of each module, and the sensitivity analysis over K (number of views) and radial constraints provides useful design guidance.

The camera pose parameterization via a look-at model with reparameterized Gaussian sampling and sigmoid-bounded spherical coordinates is technically sound and enables end-to-end gradient-based viewpoint optimization.

The overall average success rate (86.6%) is the best reported among compared methods on this RLBench subset, and large per-task gains are shown on occlusion-prone tasks (e.g., insert peg 98.0 vs 78.4 for ARP+), with only modest inference overhead (+10.7%).
weaknesses: The headline improvement over the strongest baseline is modest: 86.6% vs 84.9% for ARP+ (~1.7 points average over 18 tasks with 25 evaluation episodes each). With no statistical significance testing, error bars on the aggregate comparison, or variance analysis of the baseline, it is unclear whether the average gain is reliable. The exceptionally large gain on insert peg (+19.6 points) appears anomalous relative to other tasks and deserves verification.

The ablation design is confusing and potentially inconsistent. 'w/o Active Exploration Fine-tuning (Random Viewpoints)' drops success to 8.89% while '(Fixed Viewpoints)' yields 83.33%. It is unclear whether the random-viewpoint variant was trained at all or only evaluated; if the action policy was trained on fixed views and tested on random views, the 8.89% figure conflates a train/test mismatch with the value of view planning. This weakens the paper's central claim that task-aware view planning 'contributes dominantly' to performance.

The zero-shot generalization claim is questionable: the 'unseen' task 'Open drawer' appears essentially in-domain — the 18 training tasks include 'open drawer'/'put item in drawer' variants (Table 1), and Fig. 8 shows tasks such as 'open the top drawer' and 'put the item in the top drawer'. A true OOD evaluation would require a genuinely held-out task family, not a near-duplicate of trained tasks.

The TaskMoE ablation gain is small (86.67% vs 85.56%, ~1 point), yet the paper devotes substantial narrative to its novelty. The decoupled gating design (NG < NJ) is not directly ablated (e.g., against a standard per-task gate or NG = NJ), so the specific contribution of the proposed gating mechanism relative to generic MoE routing remains unverified.

The reward design has potential issues that are not analyzed: r0 = Lref − LTAVP with learnable weights and online normalization could permit reward hacking (e.g., the view policy selecting viewpoints that lower surrogate losses without improving actual task success). No analysis of the learned viewpoints (e.g., pose distributions, agreement with human intuition) or of failure modes of the reward is provided beyond qualitative figures.

The main configuration uses K=3 viewpoints even though the sensitivity analysis (Table 3) shows K=4 is better (55.2% vs 49.6% average on the validation tasks). The rationale for the mismatch between the tuned configuration and the final system is not explained.

Reproducibility and presentation issues: the reference list contains placeholder template entries ([1]-[6], 'frobnication' references), a text artifact ('Zhouxia') appears in Figure 3, citation [182] (Transporter Networks) is given as the source of the look-at model, and the naming is inconsistent (MVEP vs MVEPN). The critical pseudo-environment reward details are deferred to the supplement while the main text states they 'will be presented in the supplementary materials' in a form suggesting an unfinished draft.

The real-world comparison is weaker than the simulation evaluation: the baseline is Diffusion Policy rather than the strongest architectural baseline (ARP+), with only 10 trials per task and no variance reporting, and it is unclear whether the camera configurations used for DP and TAVP were matched, given TAVP's dependence on a reconstructed global point cloud.

Per-task results show regressions against ARP+ on several tasks (put in safe 78.0 vs 86.4, stack cups 64.0 vs 80.0), which the paper does not discuss; this suggests the method trades off performance on some tasks and that the aggregate gain may hide distributional shifts.
